builder_plan.scenario: You already need task-specific training and want to reduce its memory or compute cost.
builder_plan.change: Change only the training technique on a small controlled run after checking prerequisites.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current training recipe with the same model, data split, and evaluation.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Held-out quality, peak memory, training time, and full compute cost to the target quality.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Where Rounding Happens Matters: Rounding-Location Alignment Stabilizes LLM Reinforcement Learning
summary: The method replaces full-stack inference/training alignment, global precision changes, or modified RL objectives with targeted FP32 retention of intermediates at three rounding locations (RoPE, SwiGLU, residual RMSNorm) in the training stack. It costs a modest increase in training-side memory for retained FP32 intermediates and requires implementation access to the training framework's forward pass; inference engine, kernels, and learning objective remain unchanged. It can fail if applied to architectures or frameworks where the dominant train-inference mismatch arises from other operators, and its findings are validated only on Qwen-family models, so transfer to other model families or RL setups is unverified.
rationale: The technique directly addresses a real instability in RL fine-tuning of LLMs with minimal cost, but the reader does not train foundation models and would only encounter it if running BF16 RL fine-tuning, so it warrants monitoring rather than immediate adoption.
technique: Rounding-location alignment for RL training stability

claims.statement: The method replaces full-stack inference/training alignment, global precision changes, or modified RL objectives with targeted FP32 retention of intermediates at three rounding locations (RoPE, SwiGLU, residual RMSNorm) in the training stack. It costs a modest increase in training-side memory for retained FP32 intermediates and requires implementation access to the training framework's forward pass; inference engine, kernels, and learning objective remain unchanged. It can fail if applied to architectures or frameworks where the dominant train-inference mismatch arises from other operators, and its findings are validated only on Qwen-family models, so transfer to other model families or RL setups is unverified.

Aligning RoPE, SwiGLU, and residual RMSNorm rounding locations prevents the training collapse observed under the default BF16 baseline across four Qwen-family models; RoPE-path alignment alone also suffices in the studied runs.
